# Where we are {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The 90 minutes ahead

| | |
|---|---|
| **0–10** | Why OLS breaks when predictors multiply |
| **10–30** | Ridge: shrinking without choosing |

## Before class you read

**Wang, Zhu & Yu**, *Variable Selection in Macroeconomic Forecasting with Many
Predictors*, **Econometrics and Statistics**.

::: {.muted}
DOI: 10.1016/j.ecosta.2023.01.003
:::

The finding to hold on to:

> Across their comparisons, **classical forward selection was competitive with
> far more sophisticated methods.** Sophistication is not the point. Knowing
> what your selection is sensitive to is the point.

## The question for today

Thirty European countries. Eleven years. And **thirty-odd candidate predictors**
of whether a country's AI adoption translates into anything measurable.

::: {.tight}
- Which predictors matter?
- How confident are you in that list?
- Would a slightly different sample give you a different list?
:::

::: {.warn}
That last question is the one this session is really about, and it is the one
almost never asked in published work.
:::

# Why OLS breaks {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The variance of $\hat\beta$

$$\operatorname{Var}(\hat\beta_{\text{OLS}}) = \sigma^2 (X'X)^{-1}$$

As predictors become numerous or correlated, $X'X$ approaches singularity, its
inverse explodes, and so does the variance.

::: {.tight}
- $p > n$: $(X'X)^{-1}$ does not exist at all
- $p$ close to $n$: it exists and is useless
- Correlated columns: individually unidentified, jointly fine
:::

## What that looks like

You get coefficients that are:

::: {.tight}
- **large**, with alternating signs
- **unstable** — drop three rows and they move substantially
- **individually insignificant** while the model as a whole fits well
:::

::: {.check}
That last combination is the classic signature. An $F$-test that rejects while
no single $t$-test does means your predictors are fighting over the same
variance.
:::

## The bias–variance bargain

OLS is the **best linear unbiased** estimator. Note the middle word.

If we accept a little bias, we can buy a lot of variance reduction:

$$\mathbb{E}\big[(\hat\beta - \beta)^2\big] = \operatorname{Bias}^2 + \operatorname{Var}$$

::: {.check}
Every method today deliberately introduces bias. That is not a flaw being
tolerated — it is the mechanism.
:::

# Ridge {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The ridge problem

$$\hat\beta_{\text{ridge}} = \arg\min_\beta \; \|y - X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|_2^2$$

which has a closed form:

$$\hat\beta_{\text{ridge}} = (X'X + \lambda I)^{-1}X'y$$

::: {.check}
Adding $\lambda$ down the diagonal makes the matrix invertible **by
construction**. Ridge works when $p > n$; OLS does not exist there.
:::

## What ridge does to correlated predictors

Ridge **shares** a coefficient among correlated predictors rather than picking
one.

::: {.tight}
- Two identical columns → each gets half the coefficient
- Nothing is ever set exactly to zero
- Every predictor stays in the model
:::

::: {.muted}
This is the right behaviour when you believe many small effects exist, and the
wrong behaviour when you want a short list.
:::

## Ridge shrinks unevenly

In the basis of the singular vectors of $X$, ridge multiplies each direction by

$$\frac{d_j^2}{d_j^2 + \lambda}$$

where $d_j$ is the $j$-th singular value.

::: {.tight}
- Large $d_j$ — high-variance directions — barely shrink
- Small $d_j$ — the poorly determined directions — shrink hard
:::

::: {.check}
Ridge shrinks *exactly where the data are least informative*. That is why it
works, and it is the same decomposition you will meet again in Session 08.
:::

## Scaling is not optional

The penalty $\lambda\|\beta\|_2^2$ treats every coefficient identically.

A predictor measured in euros and one measured in shares get the same penalty
for wildly different economic magnitudes.

::: {.warn}
**Always standardise before penalising** — and do it *inside* the
cross-validation pipeline, or you have leaked the test fold's mean and variance
into training. Session 04's rule applies with full force here.
:::

# Lasso {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## The lasso problem

$$\hat\beta_{\text{lasso}} = \arg\min_\beta \; \|y - X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda\|\beta\|_1$$

One character changed — $\|\cdot\|_2^2$ became $\|\cdot\|_1$ — and the
behaviour changes completely.

::: {.check}
There is **no closed form**. Coefficients are found by coordinate descent, and
some arrive at exactly zero.
:::

## Why $\ell_1$ sets things to zero

Picture the constraint region:

::: {.tight}
- $\ell_2$ is a **sphere** — smooth, no corners
- $\ell_1$ is a **diamond** — corners on the axes
:::

The solution is where the residual contours first touch the region. A diamond
is most likely to be touched **at a corner**, and a corner is a point where some
coefficients are exactly zero.

::: {.muted}
Sparsity is a geometric accident of the shape of the constraint, not a
statistical principle.
:::

## Soft thresholding

With orthonormal predictors the lasso has a clean form:

$$\hat\beta_j = \operatorname{sign}(\hat\beta_j^{\text{OLS}})\left(|\hat\beta_j^{\text{OLS}}| - \lambda\right)_+$$

::: {.tight}
- Below $\lambda$ → set to **exactly zero**
- Above $\lambda$ → shrunk **toward** zero by $\lambda$
:::

::: {.warn}
Note the second line. Surviving coefficients are still biased toward zero. The
lasso is a selector *and* a shrinker, and people routinely forget the second
part when interpreting magnitudes.
:::

## What the lasso does badly

::: {.tight}
1. **Correlated groups.** Among ten correlated predictors it picks roughly one,
   near-arbitrarily, and zeroes the rest.
2. **$p > n$.** It selects at most $n$ predictors, whatever the truth.
3. **Inference.** Standard errors after selection are not valid — the data chose
   the model, and the usual formulas do not know that.
:::

::: {.warn}
"The lasso selected these six variables, and here are their p-values" is not a
sentence you may write. Session 10 is where valid post-selection inference
appears.
:::

# Elastic net {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Both penalties at once

$$\hat\beta_{\text{EN}} = \arg\min_\beta \|y - X\beta\|_2^2 + \lambda\left(\alpha\|\beta\|_1 + \tfrac{1-\alpha}{2}\|\beta\|_2^2\right)$$

::: {.tight}
- $\alpha = 1$ → lasso
- $\alpha = 0$ → ridge
- in between → both
:::

::: {.check}
The $\ell_2$ part restores the **grouping effect**: correlated predictors are
selected or dropped *together* rather than arbitrarily one-of-ten.
:::

## Two parameters to choose

You are now cross-validating over a **grid**: $\lambda$ and $\alpha$ together.

::: {.tight}
- Do it in one pipeline, one CV scheme
- Report the chosen pair, not just $\lambda$
- Expect a flat region rather than a sharp optimum
:::

::: {.muted}
A flat CV surface is information: it means the data do not strongly prefer one
degree of sparsity. Say so.
:::

# The data {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## What you are working with

```python
import pandas as pd

c = pd.read_parquet("data/spine/angle_c_country.parquet")
print(c.shape)        # (330, 33) — 30 countries x 11 years, 2014-2024
```

::: {.tight}
- `ai_use_any`, `ai_use_ml`, `cloud_use`, `ict_specialists`, `digital_intensity`
- `barrier_cost`, `barrier_skills`, `barrier_data`, `barrier_legal`
- `rd_pct_gdp`, `has_ai_strategy`
- **`aux_00` … `aux_14`** — fifteen further candidate predictors
:::

## The trap, stated plainly

::: {.warn}
**`ai_use_any` does not exist before 2021.** Not "is missing" — *does not
exist*. The survey module did not run.
:::

```python
c.groupby("time").ai_use_any.apply(lambda s: s.notna().sum())
# 2014-2020: 0    2021: 28    2022: 28    2023: 27    2024: 29
```

::: {.check}
Seven years of your panel have no outcome. A method that silently drops them
has quietly changed your research question from 2014–2024 to 2021–2024.
:::

## The second trap

The `aux_*` columns are **correlated with each other and with the real
predictors**.

That is the situation the whole session is about:

::: {.tight}
- The lasso will pick a handful
- A slightly different sample will make it pick a *different* handful
- Both lists will look convincing in a table
:::

::: {.muted}
Nobody publishes the second list. You are going to compute it.
:::

# Doing it {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Build the design matrix

```python
import numpy as np

d = c[c.time >= 2021].dropna(subset=["ai_use_any"]).copy()

drop = ["geo", "time", "flag", "ai_use_any", "ai_use_ml", "ai_use_ge3"]
X = d.drop(columns=drop).fillna(d.median(numeric_only=True))
y = d["ai_use_any"]

print(X.shape, y.shape)     # about 112 rows, 27 predictors
```

::: {.warn}
`n` is now roughly **112** with **27** predictors. That ratio is the whole
problem — and it was 330 rows before the outcome's availability was checked.
:::

## Ridge and lasso, cross-validated

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import RidgeCV, LassoCV
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold

cv = GroupKFold(5)
g  = d["geo"]

ridge = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), RidgeCV(alphas=np.logspace(-3, 3, 60)))
lasso = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                      LassoCV(cv=list(cv.split(X, y, g)), max_iter=50_000))

ridge.fit(X, y)
lasso.fit(X, y)
```

::: {.check}
Grouped by country, because two years of the same country are not independent.
Session 04's argument has not gone away.
:::

## Who survived?

```python
coef = pd.Series(lasso[-1].coef_, index=X.columns)
kept = coef[coef != 0].sort_values(key=abs, ascending=False)
print(f"{(coef != 0).sum()} of {len(coef)} predictors kept")
print(kept.round(3))
```

::: {.muted}
Look at whether any `aux_*` columns are in that list. They are noise-adjacent by
construction — if they beat a real predictor, that tells you something about how
much evidence 112 rows contains.
:::

## Elastic net over a grid

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import ElasticNetCV

en = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    ElasticNetCV(l1_ratio=[0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 0.95, 1.0],
                 cv=list(GroupKFold(5).split(X, y, g)), max_iter=50_000),
)
en.fit(X, y)
print("chosen l1_ratio:", en[-1].l1_ratio_, "| alpha:", round(en[-1].alpha_, 4))
```

::: {.check}
Report both chosen values. A chosen `l1_ratio` near 1 says the data wanted
sparsity; near 0 says they wanted sharing.
:::

# The part nobody reports {background-color="#16181A" style="color:#F7F6F3"}

## Selection stability

Resample the data. Refit. Record which predictors survive. Repeat.

```python
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV
from collections import Counter

rng = np.random.default_rng(60033)
counts = Counter()
B = 200

for _ in range(B):
    idx = rng.choice(len(X), len(X), replace=True)
    m = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LassoCV(cv=5, max_iter=50_000))
    m.fit(X.iloc[idx], y.iloc[idx])
    counts.update(X.columns[m[-1].coef_ != 0])

freq = pd.Series(counts).reindex(X.columns).fillna(0) / B
print(freq.sort_values(ascending=False).head(12).round(2))
```

## Read the selection frequencies

::: {.tight}
- **> 0.90** — robust. Reportable as "selected".
- **0.40–0.90** — genuinely uncertain. Say so.
- **< 0.40** — appeared in your one fit by luck.
:::

::: {.warn}
If your headline predictor is selected in 55% of bootstrap replicates, then a
different sample would have given you a different paper. That belongs in your
results, not in a footnote.
:::

## What to report

::: {.tight}
- The **CV scheme** and why it is grouped
- The chosen $\lambda$, and $\alpha$ if elastic net
- The selected set, **with selection frequencies**
- That coefficients are shrunk, so magnitudes are biased toward zero
- That the outcome does not exist before 2021, and what that did to $n$
:::

::: {.warn}
No p-values on lasso-selected coefficients. The data chose the model; the
standard formulas assume you did.
:::

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Not standardising | The penalty tracks units, not importance |
| Scaling outside the CV fold | Leakage; CV error too low |
| Random K-fold on this panel | Optimistic, for Session 04's reason |
| Reporting one selected set | Hides that it was near-arbitrary |
| p-values after selection | Invalid |
| Ignoring the pre-2021 gap | Silently changes the question |

## In the lab

::: {.tight}
1. Rebuild the design matrix and **confirm the 2021 cliff yourself**
2. Fit ridge, lasso and elastic net under grouped CV
3. Run the bootstrap and produce the selection-frequency table
4. Compare against Wang, Zhu & Yu: does forward selection do as well here?
5. Three sentences on what your selected set does and does not license
:::

::: {.check}
The deliverable is the **frequency table**, not the coefficient table. Anyone
can produce the second one.
:::
